# Materials and Methods

@fig-overview presents an overview of the workflow. Using time-lapse imagery, we (i) produced vegetation classification maps for 2012 and 2021 to quantify 9-year changes in *Sasa* distribution and (ii) characterised the snowmelt regime and its temporal trend from per-pixel snowmelt dates for 2011–2021, expressed as day of year (DOY). We then (iii) fitted two statistical models, a habitat suitability model of environmental potential (Model A) and an establishment model of the observed 2012–2021 transitions (Model B), and (iv) projected establishment to 2030 under explicit snowmelt scenarios using a stochastic cellular automaton based on Model B. All spatial analyses used a common 1 m grid (JGD2011 / UTM zone 53N, EPSG:6690).

![Images from a single fixed camera support two models corresponding to the two modes of *Sasa* expansion and projections of future establishment. (a) Data generation: alignment, classification, and georectification of time-lapse imagery produce vegetation maps (2012, 2021) and per-pixel snowmelt DOY (2011–2021). Terrain variables are derived from a DEM. (b) Model A: presence in 2021 and environmental conditions are used to estimate a habitat suitability surface (environmental potential; seed-dispersal stratum). (c) Model B: observed 2012→2021 transitions are modelled as a function of distance from the front and environment (rhizome stratum). Establishment is concentrated along the edges of 2012 patches, as illustrated by the orange cells in the schematic. (d) Projection: a stochastic cellular automaton applying Model B annually, updating the distance surface each year and taking snowmelt scenario s as input, yields establishment probabilities by 2030.](files/fig01_workflow.png){#fig-overview width=100%}

## Study site {#sec-study-site}

The study slope lies on the western side of Mt. Tateyama (Murodo-daira and the surrounding slopes, 2,350–3,015 m a.s.l.) in the northern Japanese Alps, within Chubu-Sangaku National Park, Toyama Prefecture. The region is among the snowiest alpine environments in the world. Airborne laser surveys at peak snow accumulation show that mean snow depth on the western slope of Mt. Tateyama increases linearly with elevation, reaching approximately 7 m at Murodo-daira, with substantially greater local depths in snowdrifts [@Iida2006JSSI]. The plateau consists of pyroclastic deposits from Tateyama Volcano, and the slopes are dissected by avalanche tracks and hollows that retain snow. Snowmelt progresses from wind-exposed ridges, typically in May–June, to snowbed hollows where snow persists into August, creating steep gradients in growing-season length over horizontal distances of tens of metres.

The vegetation forms a mosaic typical of the snowy alpine zone of central Japan: dwarf pine scrub on exposed sites, snowbed communities in late-melting hollows, tall-forb meadows on moist slopes, and deciduous shrubs (rowans, maple, and montane alder) along streams and avalanche tracks. *Sasa* forms dense stands near the lower limit of the alpine zone and occurs as scattered patches within the study slope. Although the area receives intensive tourist use via the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, visitors remain on maintained trails, and the observed slope is not directly affected by trampling. No vegetation management or *Sasa* removal took place on the slope during the study period.

## Image acquisition {#sec-image-acquisition}

We used images captured by a digital time-lapse camera (EOS 5D Mark II, Canon Inc., 21 megapixels) installed by the National Institute for Environmental Studies on the Murodo-sanso mountain lodge (approximately 2,450 m a.s.l.). Since 2010, the camera has photographed the slope hourly from 6:00 to 19:00 between April and November. For details of the installation and operation, see @Okamoto2024RSEC. Vegetation classification used images acquired in August–October of 2012 and 2021 (7 frames per year), and snowmelt detection used images from April–August of each year during 2011–2021. Data for 2019 are missing because of construction work at the mountain lodge housing the camera. Images from 2010 were excluded because a different lens gave an incompatible field of view. Snowmelt detection followed the workflow of @IdeOguma2013EcolInfom, which is based on Otsu's binarisation method [@otsu_binarization]. Detectable snowmelt dates were censored by the imaging season (approximately DOY 120–230), and pixels without valid detections, including sky and permanently occluded terrain, were treated as missing.

## Vegetation classification maps

Vegetation classification maps were produced using the three-step pipeline of @Okamoto2024RSEC.

- **Image alignment.** All frames from both years were aligned to a common reference frame by matching AKAZE local features and estimating projective transformations with RANSAC in OpenCV. Median residual misalignment between the 2012 and 2021 series was 1–2 pixels, with no systematic offset between years.
- **Vegetation classification.** Each pixel was assigned to one of 7 classes: dwarf pine (*Pinus pumila*), dwarf bamboo (*Sasa* spp.), rowans (*Sorbus sambucifolia*, *S. matsumurana*), maple (*Acer tschonoskii*), montane alder (*Alnus viridis* subsp. *maximowiczii*), other vegetation (alpine herbs and dwarf shrubs such as crowberry and avens), and no vegetation. The classifier was a convolutional recurrent neural network (Conv2D–LSTM on 5×5-pixel patches) using temporal changes in leaf colour across seasonal image sequences. Training labels comprised 216 hand-drawn polygons, delineated mainly on 2015 imagery and checked against the 2012 and 2021 image sequences. Overall accuracy in 5-fold cross-validation was 0.982 for the 2012 series and 0.975 for the 2021 series (class-specific accuracy, network architecture, and training procedures are provided in the Supplementary Information). However, cross-validation splits were made at the pixel rather than polygon level, and the same labelled polygons were applied to both years. These estimates therefore disproportionately reflect accuracy near the training polygons; classification accuracy at unseen locations farther from the training data may be lower.
- **Georectification.** Ground control points were automatically extracted from orthorectified aerial photographs and a DEM to estimate camera parameters, and images were projected onto the 1 m analysis grid using the Python package `alproj` (https://github.com/0kam/alproj) [@Okamoto2024RSEC]. Median ground-control-point residuals were approximately 2 pixels, and the raster maps were completed with a single gap-filling pass using a 3×3 modal filter.

## Quantification of *Sasa* change {#sec-sasa-change}

We overlaid the 2012 and 2021 vegetation maps (Figure S6) and calculated a transition matrix for all classes. Throughout, we distinguish three quantities: **gross expansion**, the area transitioning from non-*Sasa* to *Sasa*; **gross loss**, the area transitioning from *Sasa* to non-*Sasa*; and **net change**, their difference. Areas are reported as the sum of the actual areas of 1 m cells measured on the Earth's ellipsoid (geodesic area). These are nearly identical to nominal areas calculated as cell count × 1 m² (difference <0.1%); figure legends and model sample sizes refer to cell counts. Because *Sasa* can persist beneath shrub canopies, apparent loss may reflect canopy cover or shifts in the classification of mixed *Sasa*–shrub pixels rather than true decline. We report the destination classes of loss in the Results and address this ambiguity in the Discussion. To assess these possibilities empirically, we conducted a blind interpretation of paired images. A total of 129 samples comprised 79 stratified samples of loss cells, proportional to the composition of destination classes, 40 stable controls (20 *Sasa* in both years and 20 dwarf pine in both years), and 10 reverse transitions (dwarf pine→*Sasa*). Paired image crops from 2012 and 2021 were presented in random order with transition types concealed. Each sample included two pairs, one from the green-leaf season and one from the autumn-colour season; frames with similar image greenness were paired to reduce misinterpretation arising from differences in leaf colour between acquisition dates. The first author assigned each sample to one of four interpretation categories: *Sasa* loss, canopy cover, boundary ambiguity, or indeterminate (full design and results in the Supplementary Information).

## Snowmelt regime and trends {#sec-snowmelt}

For every 1 m cell, we compiled 10 years of annual snowmelt DOY (2011–2021, excluding the missing year 2019) and calculated (i) **snowmelt climatology**, the 2011–2021 mean snowmelt date (DOY), which averages over interannual variation to represent the prevailing snowmelt timing at each location, and (ii) a per-pixel linear trend, the slope of an ordinary least-squares regression of DOY against year. As a perennial plant, *Sasa* is expected to respond to the prevailing local snowmelt regime rather than snowmelt in any single year, so both models used snowmelt climatology as the environmental predictor. Trends were not included as predictors. Per-pixel trend estimates are noisy, with a detection limit of approximately 2 days/year as discussed below, and adding the trend to Model B did not improve prediction in held-out spatial blocks (Supplementary Information).

The trends require careful interpretation. With a 10-year record and a residual annual SD of approximately 9 days, the minimum detectable per-pixel slope is approximately 2 days/year; trends of plausible magnitude therefore cannot be detected statistically. Accordingly, trends were used only to parameterise scenarios for the 2030 projections (@sec-projection), not as evidence that a change in snowmelt had been demonstrated. Forecasting snowmelt timing itself was beyond the scope of this study.

## Statistical models {#sec-models}

We addressed the two questions set out in the Introduction, where environmental conditions permit *Sasa* and where observed establishment occurred, using two models with a shared evaluation design.

**Shared predictors.** Both models used slope, elevation, topographic position index (TPI; elevation relative to the surrounding terrain, distinguishing ridges from hollows), topographic wetness index (TWI; derived from contributing area and slope), northness (cos aspect), and eastness (sin aspect), derived from the Fundamental Geospatial Data digital elevation model (DEM) of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan [@GSIdem] and reprojected to the analysis grid, together with snowmelt climatology (@sec-snowmelt). Details of terrain-variable derivation are provided in the Supplementary Information. Aspect, a circular variable, was decomposed into northness and eastness before reprojection. Terrain roughness and terrain ruggedness index were excluded before modelling because of strong collinearity with slope (Spearman |r| = 0.93–0.97). All retained predictors had variance inflation factors below 2.3 and pairwise |r| below 0.7.

**Shared evaluation design.** A single set of spatial blocks (4 folds) was defined across the full analysis domain using `spatialsample` [@spatialsample] and used for tuning, ensemble construction, and held-out evaluation of both models. Model comparisons thus used the same evaluation areas.

### Model A: environmental potential

Model A was a habitat suitability model fitted to the 2021 *Sasa* distribution. Presences were *Sasa* cells at 1 m resolution; pseudo-absences were non-*Sasa* cells thinned to one per 5 m cell to reduce class imbalance. We tuned four algorithms in `tidysdm` [@tidysdm] by grid search with up to 18 candidates per algorithm: gradient boosted trees [@Friedman2001GBM], MaxEnt [@Philips2006MaxEnt], random forest [@Breiman2001RandForest], and generalised additive models. Candidates were selected by TSS on spatial blocks and blended using LASSO-regularised stacking [@RCranStack]. The final ensemble composition is reported in the Results. Performance is reported as the True Skill Statistic (TSS; @Allouche2006TSS) and AUC on held-out spatial blocks. The main outputs were a continuous map of habitat suitability on a 0–1 scale (the suitability surface) and response curves for each predictor. Where binarisation was needed, we used the threshold maximising TSS on held-out predictions; sensitivity of suitable area to thresholds of 0.1–0.7 is reported in the Supplementary Information. The main model used the full elevation range of the mapped slope. Results for a sensitivity variant restricting the domain to elevations below 2,560 m, the upper limit of the observed distribution, are provided in the Supplementary Information.

### Model B: establishment model

Model B directly modelled observed transitions. For all cells that were non-*Sasa* in 2012 (n = 1,197,536), the response was whether they had become *Sasa* by 2021 (establishment; n = 4,095). Predictors comprised the shared environmental variables and distance from the 2012 *Sasa* front. Distance was calculated as the Euclidean distance to the nearest cell belonging to a 2012 *Sasa* patch exceeding 5 m² in geodesic area, with patches defined by 4-neighbour connectivity. This patch-size rule prevented tiny patches arising from classification noise from dominating the estimated expansion process: because area gain through rhizome elongation is proportional to patch perimeter, tiny patches with the highest perimeter-to-area ratios have disproportionate influence.

We fitted a binomial generalised additive model (GAM; `bam` in `mgcv` [@mgcvWood]) to all eligible cells, using thin-plate spline smooths for all predictors. The distance term used a logarithmic transformation, `s(log(1 + d))`, concentrating smooth flexibility near the front, where observations were densest (criteria for specification choice and sensitivity are provided in the Supplementary Information). Model B was evaluated by leave-one-block-out refitting on the shared spatial partition. As a robustness comparison, we also fitted a gradient boosted tree ensemble to the same response, predictors, and folds. The estimated dispersal kernel is presented as mean predicted establishment probability by distance band alongside observed establishment rates.

## Projections to 2030 {#sec-projection}

Model A's suitability map describes the extent of environmentally permissive habitat, whereas rhizome expansion can proceed only from existing fronts. Applying the suitability map directly to the future would therefore greatly overestimate near-term establishment area. We instead projected establishment using a stochastic cellular automaton that applied Model B annually, and used Model A as the environmental-potential stratum corresponding to seed dispersal (@sec-risky). Projections thus arose from the expansion process itself rather than from a suitability threshold.

Starting from the observed 2021 distribution, we repeated the following steps for each year from 2022 to 2030. (i) Recalculate the distance surface from the current simulated distribution using the same 5 m² patch rule as in model fitting. (ii) Evaluate the 9-year establishment probability $p_9$ from Model B for every unoccupied cell and convert it to an annual probability: $p_1 = 1 - (1 - p_9)^{1/9}$. (iii) Draw establishment independently for each cell from a Bernoulli distribution, retaining occupancy once established (assuming no loss within the 9-year period). For computational efficiency, the environmental component of the linear predictor was precomputed for each scenario × year, and only the distance term was updated within the simulation; this decomposition is exact (Supplementary Information). We ran 200 replicates per scenario and report per-cell establishment probabilities (means across replicates) and expected new establishment area (the sum of probability × cell area). The latter requires no binarisation threshold.

**Scenarios.** Snowmelt climatology was shifted linearly by s × (year − 2016), where 2016 is the midpoint of the averaging period. In the main text, we report s = 0 (no change, consistent with the non-significant trend) and s = −0.71 days/year (the point estimate of the observed trend); s = −2.24 days/year (the lower confidence limit) is reported as an extreme scenario in the Supplementary Information. These are scenarios conditional on the observed decade, not forecasts of snowmelt. Shifts were spatially uniform because per-pixel trend estimates are dominated by noise and cannot be directly extrapolated (@sec-snowmelt). The uniform shift is an approximation, justified in the Supplementary Information alongside an assessment of the spatial structure of per-pixel trends.

**Validation.** We conducted three checks. (1) *Hindcast*: we tested whether simulations initialised from the 2012 distribution reproduced the observed 2012–2021 gross expansion. Because Model B was fitted to the same interval, this is a calibration check rather than independent validation. (2) *Independent spatial validation*: for each spatial block, we refitted Model B excluding that block and scored the hindcast only within the omitted block. (3) *Structural sensitivity*: we quantified changes in the projections when the 5 m² patch rule was removed from distance updates and when annualisation was replaced by the first-order approximation $p_9/9$.

## Risk to alpine communities {#sec-risky}

We present two risk strata corresponding to the two modes of *Sasa* expansion. The **near-term rhizome stratum** comprises cellular-automaton establishment probabilities restricted to cells classified as other vegetation in 2021, a class dominated by alpine herbs and including snowbed communities of conservation concern, summarised as expected establishment area. To identify the communities at risk, we overlaid the 1:25,000 vegetation GIS map compiled under the National Survey on the Natural Environment by the Biodiversity Center of Japan, Nature Conservation Bureau, Ministry of the Environment (Hokuriku block) [@MOEvegmap2024] and cross-tabulated expected establishment area by mapped community. The scale mismatch between 1:25,000 polygons and the 1 m grid is addressed as a limitation in the Discussion. The **seed-dispersal stratum** represents environmental potential in 2021, namely areas of high habitat suitability in Model A. Because establishment from seed is not constrained by the modelled distance process, environmental potential provides a first approximation of the area that could be exposed; unmeasured factors such as soils and constraints on seedling establishment are not accounted for. Field validation of community composition and assessment of rare-species occurrence within risk areas remain future work.

## Software and reproducibility

All analyses used R 4.5.2 (terra, sf, tidymodels/tidysdm, stacks, spatialsample, mgcv) in a scripted, non-interactive pipeline with fixed random seeds. Code and data will be archived at [TODO: Zenodo DOI].
